content_list.content_text: Since the release of Jaws (1975), summer box office champions (or blockbusters) have been aimed at younger audiences. Epics and dramas for adults are a thing of the past: recent decades have been dominated by family entertainment. For the industry, this shift has meant increased profits that go beyond box office receipts, ranging from toys and other merchandise to sales of videos, DVDs, and Blu-rays, which often generate more revenue than the theatrical release itself.

information.contentTitle: Scenes from Pirates of the Caribbean: At World's End
information.contentText: Although it has never been officially confirmed, there are strong indications that the series was influenced by, and perhaps loosely based on, the Monkey Island video game series. Ted Elliott, one of the two screenwriters of the four films in the Pirates of the Caribbean series, reportedly wrote a film adaptation of the third game in the Monkey Island series, titled The Curse of Monkey Island (presumably based on the game of the same name), which was canceled before its official announcement, three years before the release of the first film.

content_list.title: The Rules (Guidelines) of Adventure — The Pirates of the Caribbean
content_list.description: Pirates of the Caribbean: The Curse of the Black Pearl shows the best of the adventure genre by using key elements of the genre as fundamental building blocks of the story and character design. In this video, the LFTS team explores four critical components of classic adventure films, dives deep into the ways Pirates uses them as basic design rules (or guidelines), and shows why remixing the genre with an unexpected element helps make the film fun, scary, and surprising.

movie.original_title: Pirates of the Caribbean: The Curse of the Black Pearl
movie.overview: Jack Sparrow, a freewheeling 18th-century pirate, quarrels with a rival pirate bent on pillaging Port Royal. When the governor's daughter is kidnapped, Sparrow decides to help the girl's love save her.
movie.tagline: Prepare to be blown out of the water.

content_list.content_text: Disney understood the value of family entertainment from the start. Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs (1938) was the most successful film of the year, its hand-drawn animation setting a trend that would last almost 50 years. Disney's last conventional cartoon to dominate the box office was The Lion King (1994), a year before a newcomer that came out of nowhere entered the fray.

quote.quote: One of the few occasions when it's OK to enjoy something for being smart and dumb at the same time, mainly because it's undeniably fun.
quote.author: Todd Gilchrist on Transformers

content_list.content_text: No studio has dominated family entertainment as completely in recent decades as Pixar. Although it became a subsidiary of The Walt Disney Company in 2006, its brand is so strong that it is still regarded as an independent creative entity. In the films it has produced since 1995, its signature blend of dazzling animation with smart, emotionally engaging screenplays that appeal to all ages has won near-unanimous acclaim from critics and audiences alike.

information.contentTitle: Scenes from The Lord of the Rings: The Return of the King
information.contentText: The Return of the King is widely regarded as one of the greatest and most influential films ever made. The film received numerous accolades; at the 76th Academy Awards, it won all eleven awards for which it was nominated, tying the record for the most Academy Awards won by a single film.

content_list.content_text: In the Ice Age (2002) series, from Blue Sky Studios, and the Shrek (2001) series, from DreamWorks, the originality of their first films stood out — especially in Shrek, with its deconstruction of fairy tales. The hand-drawn animation of The Princess and the Frog (2009) marked a dazzling return to a classic style that Disney had practically abandoned. Directors such as Sylvain Chomet (b. 1963) and Hayao Miyazaki (b. 1941), at Studio Ghibli, took on the task of filling this gap.

content_list.title: Peter Jackson's Masterpiece
content_list.description:
Like the trilogy written by J. R. R. Tolkien, Peter Jackson's adaptation of The Lord of the Rings should be considered a single work, albeit a very long one. Seen in sequence, the three films form an almost perfect whole, from the spectacular prologue to the epic list of credits, a true record-breaker. Everything about this film is unprecedented in the history of cinema. The three parts were shot over a continuous period of 16 months. And the series' incredible popularity more than lived up to all expectations. It is estimated to have earned almost three billion dollars at the box office, more than any other trilogy, beating even the Star Wars blockbusters. According to some experts' estimates, DVD sales amount to at least the same figure, not to mention the exploitation of a line of licensed products, which means that Middle-earth's GDP rivals that of many real countries. Fortunately, Jackson managed to stun not only the accountants but also the critics. Each film outdid the previous one on best-of lists, and the three together racked up no fewer than 30 Oscar nominations, taking home 17 statuettes.

If you have seen all three films, you won't be surprised to learn that they won the Oscar for visual effects. They are all packed with monsters and battles that become more impressive with each installment. Even so, it was the tragic figure of Gollum that managed to capture audiences' imagination. Based on movements stored in the computer and on the voice of actor Andy Serkis (b. 1964) — who would become a benchmark in motion capture and, a few years later, would play Caesar in the new Planet of the Apes trilogy (2011-2017) — the screen Gollum was entirely digital and yet as convincing as a flesh-and-blood character.

Perhaps that is Jackson's greatest achievement: remembering that cutting-edge special effects and technical mastery are not enough to make a great film. Although its leads are hobbits, elves, and wizards, all the characters are deeply human. Gollum has regrets, tries to be good, and taunts Sam, the "fat hobbit." The wizard Gandalf, played to perfection by Ian McKellen (b. 1939), is at times paternalistic and even mischievous, but never loses his aura of power and authority. And the hobbits Frodo (wide-eyed Elijah Wood) and Sam (Sean Astin) start out as brave but naive adventurers until they attain the status of true heroes. Almost as memorable as the characters is the setting. The trilogy was produced in Jackson's homeland, New Zealand, and very little digital magic was needed to create the dazzling landscapes. One of the most memorable scenes of the spectacular The Lord of the Rings: The Return of the King (2003) is the lighting of the beacons as the music swells. The camera simply travels from one mountaintop to the next as the warning signal is lit and surges against the sky. Simply marvelous.

It is also remarkable that Jackson and his co-writers Fran Walsh (b. 1959) and Philippa Boyens (b. 1962) managed to extract a gripping, fast-paced narrative from such a dense and seemingly impenetrable source. Even more remarkable is the fact that even the book's most hardcore fans loved the film. In the short, dramatic prologue, we learn that Sauron, the embodiment of evil, poured all his power into forging a ring, which was lost in an epic battle against an alliance of men and elves. The ring eventually ends up in the hands of the little hobbit Frodo Baggins. This is where the story begins. Frodo agrees to destroy it and thereby defeat Sauron once and for all. However, the ring can only be destroyed if it is cast into the volcanic heart of Mount Doom, which lies, of course, deep inside enemy territory. He sets out on this perilous journey in the company of a group of devoted hobbits, elves, dwarves, and men, including the wizard Gandalf and the mysterious Aragorn (Viggo Mortensen). Betrayal, bloodshed, and battles end up splitting the group, and Frodo, with Sam (and later with Gollum), sets off for the volcano alone, while the others prepare to stand against Sauron in a battle that will shake Middle-earth.

Despite the breadth of the canvas Jackson paints, the essence of his work is people, their relationships, and the decisions they must make. Friendship and self-sacrifice are strongly present, as is a sense of mortality. The final scenes make it clear that victory may be noble, yet may still come from an extremely painful personal sacrifice. Tolkien served in the trenches of World War I, and it is hard not to draw parallels between his experiences and the tone of melancholy that ultimately surrounds the final part of the trilogy. For many, the heart of the film lies not in the scenes of bravery but in a quiet moment in which Gandalf consoles Frodo, distraught at having to witness such terrible times. "So do all who live to see such times," says the wizard, "but that is not for them to decide. All we have to decide is what to do with the time that is given to us." It is moments like this that raise Jackson's film to the status of a masterpiece.
content_list.credits: Summary based on the text by Philip Hall, published in the book 1001 Movies You Must See Before You Die

content_list.content_text: Disney's most successful films of the first decade of the 21st century began, incongruous as it may seem, with an amusement park ride. Inspired by the last ride of its kind designed with Disney's funding, producer Jerry Bruckheimer turned it into the Pirates of the Caribbean franchise.

The first film, Pirates of the Caribbean: The Curse of the Black Pearl (2003), proved to be a surprisingly fun summer hit that harked back to the swashbuckling adventures of Hollywood's golden age, with the eccentric touch of Johnny Depp (b. 1963) as the permanently drunk Captain Jack Sparrow.

information.contentTitle: Scenes from Harry Potter and the Sorcerer's Stone
information.contentText: All the films are on the list of the 100 highest-grossing films of all time (in dollars and not adjusted for inflation), with Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows – Part 2 being the franchise's highest-grossing film, ranking thirteenth worldwide. Filming began in California, at Hollywood studios. Although the author is British, the Harry Potter film saga was produced entirely by Hollywood, with editing done in California and visual effects produced by the Hollywood industry.

content_list.content_text: Two literary sources were behind the decade's most successful franchises. J. K. Rowling's Harry Potter series got off to a shaky start thanks to the bland direction of Chris Columbus (b. 1958), but gained momentum with the dark Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (2004), directed by Alfonso Cuarón (b. 1961).

quote.quote: How far are you willing to go to save her? - I'd die for her! - Oh good! No worries then.
quote.author: Jack Sparrow (Johnny Depp) and Will Turner III (Orlando Bloom) in Pirates of the Caribbean

content_list.content_text: Meanwhile, Peter Jackson (b. 1961) was making the impressive The Lord of the Rings trilogy (2001-2003), brilliantly adapted by Jackson himself, Fran Walsh (b. 1959), and Philippa Boyens. Clever screenplays were unfortunately left out of the laughable (but hugely successful) Star Wars: Episode I – The Phantom Menace (1999), Star Wars: Episode II – Attack of the Clones (2002), and Star Wars: Episode III – Revenge of the Sith (2005), which continued George Lucas's (b. 1944) Star Wars saga.

information.contentText: The United States Armed Forces and General Motors (GM) lent vehicles and aircraft during filming, which saved the production money and added realism to the battle scenes. Hasbro's promotional campaign for the film included deals with several companies; the publicity included a viral marketing campaign, coordinated releases of comics, toys, and prequel books, as well as product placement deals with companies such as GM, Burger King, and eBay.

content_list.content_text: Other dominant forces at the box office during this period were the revitalized comic book publishers DC and Marvel. With the success of X-Men (2000), Spider-Man (2002), and Iron Man (2008), Marvel was now able to finance its own productions, starting a trend that would dominate the box office over the next decade. DC got off to a slightly later start, but Batman Begins (2005) and The Dark Knight (2008), both directed by Christopher Nolan (b. 1970), set the standard for future comic book adaptations.

content_list.title: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban: The Film That Set the Tone for the Franchise
content_list.description:
Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban, as cinema, is one of the best in the series, because it represents a great leap forward from its predecessors. As an adaptation, however, it is somewhat disappointing because of the film's lack of fidelity to the work that gave rise to it. But since we know that literature and cinema are two completely different languages, let us analyze the film from a cinematic point of view.

Chris Columbus, director of the two previous adventures, this time takes on only the role of producer, worn out after so much work. So the Mexican director Alfonso Cuarón, best known for Y tu mamá también (2001), was called in to helm this third adventure. Right from the start, it was clear this would be a difficult job, since the third book is one of the most complex and challenging in the series, not only because of its more mature plot, but because it is here that the characters begin to deal more intensely with their teenage feelings. Fortunately, Cuarón overcame all these obstacles and created one of the best films in the series, more fun and darker. Despite working with the same crew as the previous films, Cuarón makes the production evolve in many respects, starting with the look. While in the first films the costumes, though creative, felt somewhat repetitive, the director made a wise choice in letting the leads wear their own clothes, and this choice works perfectly, since we feel the actors are more at ease in their roles. This gives the film a more modern look, as well as making it more relatable to most of its teenage fans.

And if there is one thing Cuarón does well, it is putting his stamp on the film without making it feel "too auteurist." Using his camera more intensely than Columbus, the director opts for close-ups and creative movements, as well as wider shots that convey all the beauty and grandeur of the Hogwarts settings. The director emphasizes the empty, gloomy atmosphere of the landscapes, always overcast, which help create the ideal dark tone. Cuarón also gives the film a delightful pace, making it far less tedious than the first two. The customary opening at the Dursleys' house, for example, is quick, but it clearly defines what Potter is now: someone who is growing up, who is starting to take on teenage traits (notice how he is almost always irritated) — in short, he is beginning to mature.

The new elements introduced also make the film much more appealing. This time, magical creatures appear in greater numbers, ranging from Hippogriffs (a kind of cross between a horse and an eagle), through a boggart, to the Dementors, beings that suck out people's souls. Once again, the film stands out for the number of well-known names from British film and theater. While Maggie Smith and Alan Rickman need no praise, there are some new additions, such as Michael Gambon, who replaces the late Richard Harris as Albus Dumbledore. Gambon brings a much more active air to the character, erasing the sluggish image Harris had built for the wizard. David Thewlis plays Remus Lupin with great warmth, while Gary Oldman delivers a fantastic portrayal of Sirius Black, the prisoner of the title.

And as already mentioned, Daniel Radcliffe, Rupert Grint, and Emma Watson appear much more at ease in their roles, especially Radcliffe, who here began to show his dramatic talent, embodying all of the young wizard's anguish and fears. And even with its considerable drop in pace in the last 20 minutes, Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban established itself as one of the great entries in the series, the one that will forever be remembered for the new face it gave the young wizard's adventures.
content_list.credits: Summary based on the article "Crítica | Harry Potter e o Prisioneiro de Azkaban" ("Review | Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban"), by Rafael W. Oliveira in Plano Crítico.

content_list.content_text: In Avatar (2009), the most commercially successful film ever made up to that point (it would be surpassed ten years later by Avengers: Endgame (2019)), James Cameron (b. 1954) delivered a stunning 3D spectacle, starting a trend of 3D films in the years that followed, though few of them would manage to match its brilliance and good use of the technology. The film also carried a message about protecting the environment, in contrast to most hits of the genre.
content_list.content_credits: Summary based on the text by Ian Haydn Smith, published in the book "Cinema: The Whole Story" by Philip Kemp

movies.title: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban
movies.original_title: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban
movies.overview: Harry, Ron and Hermione return to Hogwarts for another magic-filled year. Harry comes face to face with danger yet again, this time in the form of escaped convict, Sirius Black—and turns to sympathetic Professor Lupin for help.
In the 22nd century, a paraplegic Marine is dispatched to the moon Pandora on a unique mission, but becomes torn between following orders and protecting an alien civilization.
movies.title: Avatar
Pirates of the Caribbean: The Curse of the Black Pearl
movies.original_title: Pirates of the Caribbean: The Curse of the Black Pearl
movies.overview: Jack Sparrow, a freewheeling 18th-century pirate, quarrels with a rival pirate bent on pillaging Port Royal. When the governor's daughter is kidnapped, Sparrow decides to help the girl's love save her.

movies.title: Transformers
movies.overview: Young teenager, Sam Witwicky becomes involved in the ancient struggle between two extraterrestrial factions of transforming robots – the heroic Autobots and the evil Decepticons. Sam holds the clue to unimaginable power and the Decepticons will stop at nothing to retrieve it.

movies.title: The Lord of the Rings: The Fellowship of the Ring
movies.overview: Young hobbit Frodo Baggins, after inheriting a mysterious ring from his uncle Bilbo, must leave his home in order to keep it from falling into the hands of its evil creator. Along the way, a fellowship is formed to protect the ringbearer and make sure that the ring arrives at its final destination: Mt. Doom, the only place where it can be destroyed.
movies.original_title: The Lord of the Rings: The Fellowship of the Ring

movies.title: Star Wars: Episode I - The Phantom Menace
movies.overview: Anakin Skywalker, a young slave strong with the Force, is discovered on Tatooine. Meanwhile, the evil Sith have returned, enacting their plot for revenge against the Jedi.
movies.original_title: Star Wars: Episode I - The Phantom Menace

movies.overview: After being bitten by a genetically altered spider, nerdy high school student Peter Parker is endowed with amazing powers to become the Amazing superhero known as Spider-Man.
movies.title: Spider-Man

movies.overview: Hancock is a down-and-out superhero who's forced to employ a PR expert to help repair his image when the public grows weary of all the damage he's inflicted during his lifesaving heroics. The agent's idea of imprisoning the antihero to make the world miss him proves successful, but will Hancock stick to his new sense of purpose or slip back into old habits?
movies.title: Hancock
King Kong
movies.overview: In 1933 New York, an overly ambitious movie producer coerces his cast and hired ship crew to travel to mysterious Skull Island, where they encounter Kong, a giant ape who is immediately smitten with the leading lady.

When Ethan Hunt, the leader of a crack espionage team whose perilous operation has gone awry with no explanation, discovers that a mole has penetrated the CIA, he's surprised to learn that he's the No. 1 suspect. To clear his name, Hunt now must ferret out the real double agent and, in the process, even the score.
movies.title: Mission: Impossible
The Dark Knight
movies.overview: Batman raises the stakes in his war on crime. With the help of Lt. Jim Gordon and District Attorney Harvey Dent, Batman sets out to dismantle the remaining criminal organizations that plague the streets. The partnership proves to be effective, but they soon find themselves prey to a reign of chaos unleashed by a rising criminal mastermind known to the terrified citizens of Gotham as the Joker.

In the year 180, the death of emperor Marcus Aurelius throws the Roman Empire into chaos.  Maximus is one of the Roman army's most capable and trusted generals and a key advisor to the emperor.  As Marcus' devious son Commodus ascends to the throne, Maximus is set to be executed.  He escapes, but is captured by slave traders.  Renamed Spaniard and forced to become a gladiator, Maximus must battle to the death with other men for the amusement of paying audiences.
movies.title: Gladiator
